title: Refuting Unsound Attacks | Sicilian Defense: Tal Gambit | GM Naroditsky’s Top Theory Speedrun
openingName: Sicilian Defense: McDonnell (f4) — Tal Gambit refutation

moves.spoken: White lunges with f4 — a legitimate but slightly dubious try, because it invites an immediate central strike.
We punish it with d5 at once. This is precisely why the Grand Prix Attack is supposed to start with the knight to c3 — to stop this very move. Skip it, and d5 is the refutation.
After the capture we do NOT slide into a Scandinavian with the queen — that would throw away the whole point of d5.
teaches: don’t recapture with the queen here

moves.spoken: Instead the knight to f6. White can't just hold the extra pawn with c4, because e6 undermines it and Black gets tremendous positional compensation — in fact the better game.
So we safely recapture on d5, and here the queen would sit far more securely than in a normal Scandinavian — White has no second knight to hit it from c3.
teaches: the point: no Nc3 available to harass the queen

moves.spoken: The f4-pawn hangs, but grabbing it isn't the spirit of the line. The prudent move is to drop the knight back to b6 — after which a later c4 nearly traps the bishop and forces an awkward check. And we're glad to keep White's dark-squared bishop terrible, hemmed in by its own f4-pawn.
teaches: don’t contort for a pawn you want left on the board

moves.spoken: The knight to b6 is the practical choice, forcing the bishop to decide. That f4-pawn is actually in our favor — it dries up White's kingside and buries his bishop — and we own the d4-square, which is the whole job of the c5-pawn.
teaches: a cramping enemy pawn can be your asset

moves.spoken: Out comes the sacrifice on f7 — not entirely stupid, but just as clearly unsound. These are exactly the tries people struggle to refute, so let's do it cleanly.

We take, and the refutation is castling by hand. Since the king has moved we build the shelter from scratch — clear the bishop, swing a rook to f8, tuck the king to g8. Short term, the f3-knight eyes e5, but any knight check we simply answer by stepping the king to g8; we only avoid the blunder of the bishop to g4.
plans: develop the kingside, then Rf8 and Kg8

moves.spoken: g6 is the classy move — get the kingside out so the king feels safe. There's no rush to develop the other knight yet.
teaches: safety first when up a piece

moves.spoken: The bishop to g7, and even a knight check we'd meet calmly, because White is simply out of attackers — the c1-bishop is buried and the c3-knight has no prospects. Next comes the rook to f8 and the manual castling is complete.
teaches: count the attackers — the defense holds

moves.spoken: White has to throw in f5 to keep any hope alive; its point is to rip open the file. Taking with the bishop plays into his hands — it runs into g4 and a crushing double check. If we capture, we capture with the pawn.
teaches: open-file sac: capture with the pawn, not the bishop

moves.spoken: So we take with the pawn — the principled choice. Don't fear ghosts: if there's no forced mate, an uncomfortable-looking king is nothing to be afraid of.
teaches: no forced mate means no reason to panic

moves.spoken: g4 just loses on the spot — pure trickery — so of course we don't take it.
We follow through with the rook to f8: castling by hand is complete, and the win won't be far behind.
